learningObjectives.title: Probability and outcomes: scales, notation and relative frequency
Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events; probabilities summing to 1

questions.q: On the probability scale, all probabilities take values in which range?
questions.explain: A probability is always a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

questions.q: What is the probability of an event that is certain to happen?
questions.explain: An event that is certain has a probability of exactly 1.

questions.q: What is the probability of an event that is impossible?
questions.explain: An impossible event cannot occur, so its probability is 0.

questions.q: The probability that it rains tomorrow is 0.3. What is the probability that it does not rain?
questions.explain: The probability of an event not happening is 1 minus the probability it happens, so 1 - 0.3 = 0.7.

questions.q: Two events are mutually exclusive if they:
options: cannot both happen at the same time
have probabilities that sum to more than 1
questions.explain: Mutually exclusive events have no outcomes in common and cannot occur simultaneously.

questions.q: For a set of mutually exclusive and exhaustive events, the sum of their probabilities is:
options: equal to the number of events
questions.explain: Exhaustive events cover every possible outcome, so their probabilities add up to 1.

questions.q: A die is rolled 200 times and a six appears 40 times. What is the relative frequency of rolling a six?
questions.explain: Relative frequency = frequency divided by total trials = 40/200 = 0.2.

questions.q: How is the expected frequency of an outcome calculated?
options: probability multiplied by the number of trials
probability divided by the number of trials
number of trials divided by probability
probability added to the number of trials
questions.explain: Expected frequency = probability of the outcome times the number of trials.

questions.q: A fair six-sided die is rolled 300 times. How many sixes would you expect?
For two independent events A and B, P(A and B) is equal to:
questions.explain: For independent events the probability of both occurring is the product of their individual probabilities.

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed twice. What is the probability of getting two heads?
questions.explain: The tosses are independent, so P(H and H) = 1/2 times 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.q: A bag contains 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are red?
questions.explain: Without replacement, P(red then red) = 3/5 times 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10.

questions.q: On a tree diagram, the probabilities on the branches coming from a single point must:
options: add up to the number of branches
questions.explain: The branches from a point represent all possible outcomes, so their probabilities sum to 1.

questions.q: To find the probability of a particular path along a tree diagram, you should:
options: multiply the probabilities along the branches
add the probabilities along the branches
subtract the probabilities along the branches
divide the probabilities along the branches
questions.explain: Probabilities are multiplied along the branches of a single path (AND), while separate paths are added (OR).

questions.q: In set notation, A ∩ B represents:
options: the elements in both A and B
the elements in A or B or both
the elements in neither A nor B
questions.explain: The intersection A ∩ B contains only the elements common to both sets.

questions.q: In set notation, A ∪ B represents:
options: the elements in A or B or both
the elements in both A and B only
the elements not in A or B
the elements in A but not B
questions.explain: The union A ∪ B contains every element belonging to A, to B, or to both.

questions.q: The notation A' (A prime) in a Venn diagram means:
options: the intersection of A and B
questions.explain: A' is the complement of A: everything in the universal set that is not in A.

questions.q: In a class of 30, 18 study French, 12 study Spanish and 5 study both. What is the probability a student chosen at random studies neither?
questions.explain: Students studying at least one = 18 + 12 - 5 = 25, so 5 study neither, giving 5/30 = 1/6.

questions.q: For two mutually exclusive events A and B, P(A or B) is equal to:
questions.explain: Because mutually exclusive events cannot overlap, their combined probability is the sum of the two probabilities.
